title: Tokenization-to-Egress Latency Telemetry Dossier
body:
Purpose:
This is a working dossier capturing a focused end-to-end trace analysis that attributes observed tail latency (p95/p99) to fine-grained stages from client-side serialization through model kernel emits to final egress. Goal is to identify the smallest set of interventions that reduce p95/p99 by >=20% for our default hosted model profile without regressing p50.

Dataset & sampling notes:
- Traces collected between 2024-11-10 and 2024-11-16.
- Total traces: 150k requests (sampled uniformly across customers but weighted to production traffic: 70% hosted, 30% dedicated).
- Sampling filter: successful completions only (HTTP 200), requests with >1k tokens excluded (outlier treatment), keep coldstart flags.
- Trace resolution: per-stage span timings emitted by runtime v2.4 (includes tokenization, input-serialize, routing, queue-wait, kv-cache-lookup, decoder-kernel, kv-cache-store, postprocess, egress-serialize).
- Cohorts: seqlen buckets (<=32, 33-128, 129-512), coldstart vs warm, batch-size 1 vs batch-size >=2.

High-level quantiles (aggregated across cohorts):
- p50: 78 ms
- p95: 342 ms
- p99: 890 ms
Notes: distribution is heavy-tailed; p50 dominated by warm, short-seq requests; p99 dominated by coldstart + long-seq + kv-miss interactions.

Per-stage median/quantiles (all values in ms, per-request):
- client-serialize: p50 1, p95 4, p99 12
- network-ingress (front-door): p50 8, p95 25, p99 95
- input-tokenize: p50 2, p95 7, p99 20
- router-decision: p50 1, p95 3, p99 10
- queue-wait: p50 6, p95 80, p99 420
- kv-cache-lookup: p50 0.8, p95 18, p99 120
- decoder-kernel (emit path): p50 40, p95 110, p99 220
- kv-cache-store: p50 0.7, p95 9, p99 45
- postprocess (detokenize + safety filter): p50 2.5, p95 9.5, p99 37
- egress-serialize: p50 1, p95 4, p99 8
- network-egress: p50 7, p95 20, p99 60

Key observations and decomposed drivers: 
1) Queue-wait & kv-cache-lookup dominate the tail.
- At p99, queue-wait and kv-cache-lookup together account for ~60% of tail latency on long-seq & coldstart traces. Many p99 traces show a queue spike happening concurrently with a KV miss cascade.
- Hypothesis: transient GPU contention (work-stealing + burstros) causes request to fall back into longer queuing on some workers; subsequent deserialized requests hit cold KV state requiring remote retrievals.

2) Network ingress/egress variability is non-negligible at tail (CDN/region variance).
- A subset of p99 traces (~18%) correlate with cross-region routing events (front-door re-resolve), manifested as both high ingress and egress latency.

3) Decoder kernel scales predictably for warm short workloads, but p95->p99 divergence grows with seqlen and batch-size mismatch.
- When batch-size is expected to be >1 but incoming traffic arrives as many singletons, GPU kernel underutilization causes more per-token amortized kernel overhead.

Trace archetypes (from clustering of p99 traces):
- Type A (KV-miss cascade): long-seq, coldstart worker, queue spike -> remote KV fetch -> decoder stalls -> p99 ~1.1s
- Type B (Network blip): short-seq but severe front-door ingress sickness -> p99 ~0.9s dominated by ingress/egress
- Type C (Kernel tail): warm worker but long-seq + singleton -> kernel overhead + postprocess -> p99 ~0.8s

Evidence & screenshots: (referenced telemetry plots in linked_artifacts). Inline summary: KV miss cascade traces show repeated "kv-remote-fetch" spans stacking; queue-wait in these traces is frequently >250ms.

Repro experiments run locally (microbenchmarks):
- Simulated 1000 warm requests, seqlen 200, batch mix 60/40 singleton/batch 8: observed p95=180ms p99=410ms on dev cluster (matches production-shaped relative ratios).
- Injected artificial 100ms KV remote latency: p99 increased by ~310ms and queue spike frequency doubled.
- Forced gateway re-resolve (DNS TTL expiration): ~22% of test runs saw an ingress bump >200ms causing p99 shifts.

Initial hypotheses (ranked):
1) KV cache cold-miss cascading under transient contention is the largest single reducible driver for p99.
2) Worker scheduling/packing heuristics allow pathological queueing under certain traffic spikes (mismatch between expected batching profile and real arrival).
3) Edge/front-door routing issues amplify tail for a non-trivial subset — mitigatable with region pinning/route fault tolerance.

Proposed interventions & expected impact (estimate ranges):
- E1: Aggressive local-KV preload for recently-assigned workers (warmup on new worker allocation): expected p99 reduction 15-35% on Type A traces.
- E2: Queue admission control: enforce a small concurrency cap per worker plus fastreject/fallback routing to a spare pool to reduce queue-wait tail: expected p99 reduction 10-25%, small p50 impact.
- E3: Provide a short-lived per-request KV read cache in runtime (L0 local-store for current request window) to avoid repeated remote fetches for same request slice: expected p99 reduction 5-15, implementation complexity high.
- E4: Front-door improvements: jittered DNS TTL and smarter region affinity to avoid ingress blips: expected p99 reduction 5-10 on affected traces.
- E5: Kernel batching hinting: route singletons to a low-latency fastpath that avoids waiting for batch formation; expected to lower kernel-related tail by 8-20% for Type C.

Short-term action items (next 2 weeks):
- A1: Gather a 48h dense-trace capture focused only on cold-launch events (status: scheduled, assignee Ravi). Linear: RD-4721.
- A2: Implement and A/B test a conservative local-KV prefetch shim in runtime (prototype PR: linked). Owner: Lena.
- A3: Add a per-worker short histogram for queue-wait (5ms bins up to 1s) to detect early signs of pathological queues. Owner: Jon.
- A4: Engage Edge infra to correlate ingress anomalies with control plane events (ticket created to infra).

Longer-term experiments (quarterly):
- L1: Rework scheduling policy to consider per-worker KV hotness and expected batch shapes (requires simulation + canary on Dedicated).
- L2: Explore persistent local-KV (RAM-backed hugepages) for high-throughput pools to reduce remote fetches.
- L3: Adaptive routing based on per-route tail-sensitivity (cost-aware, region affinity).

Open questions (to resolve during in_review):
- What percent of KV misses are due to worker reassignment vs explicit cache evictions? (need metrics hook).
- Are there hot prefixes (token sequences) that trigger more remote reads? If yes, can we proactively prime them?
- What are the cost trade-offs for local persistent KV vs remote fetches at 95th percentile?

Quick win experiments to schedule now (1 week):
- QW1: Deploy fastpath for singleton batch kernel (feature-flagged) to a small serving pool; measure p95/p99 for short-seq workload.
- QW2: Implement a short TTL local-KV warmup on new worker spin-up (cheap: start with ephemeral cache entries for last 1000 keys).

Appendix: sample anomaly trace (condensed):
- request_id: trace-20241111-17-0a3c
- seq_len: 214
- coldstart: true
- timeline (ms): ingress 27 | queue 312 | kv-lookup 98 | decoder 220 | kv-store 12 | postproc 9 | egress 18 => total 696 ms
- notes: KV-lookup spans show two remote GETs; first returned multi-chunk payload causing decoder backpressure.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally an operational, somewhat-scrappy dossier (we want actionable experiments rather than exhaustive academic analysis). Please add concrete counter-proposals inline or in comments.
- If you have a simple script that reproduces KV miss cascades at scale, drop it into the linked PR or attach here.

Signed-off-by: Maya Chen (eng-serving-runtime)
